The disparity in pharmaceutical costs between America and other countries is glaringly unacceptable. It's time to address this issue head-on.

1. Eliquis (Apixaban) - Blood Thinner
   - U.S. Price: Approximately $7,100 per year
   Other Countries:  
     - Canada: ~$900 per year.  
     - France: ~$650 per year.  
     - Germany: ~$63 for a 30-day supply.  

2. Ozempic (Semaglutide) - Diabetes/Weight Loss
   - U.S. Price: Around $1,000 per unit (monthly dose).  
   Other Countries:  
     - Europe: ~$80 per unit.  
     - Canada/Latin America: 4-5x cheaper, approximately $200-$250 per unit.  

3. Humira (Adalimumab) - Autoimmune Diseases
   - U.S. Price: Can exceed $6,000 per month for brand-name versions.  
   - Other Countries:  
     - Switzerland/Europe: Significantly lower, often 50-70% less due to generic availability and price caps.  

4. Januvia (Sitagliptin) - Diabetes
   - U.S. Price: ~$547 for a 30-day supply.  
   - Other Countries:  
     - France: ~$16 for a 30-day

5. Harvoni (Ledipasvir/Sofosbuvir) - Hepatitis C
   - U.S. Price: Around $94,500 for a 12-week course (based on 2017 data).  
   - Other Countries:  
     - Australia/Canada: Up to 60-80% lower, approximately $20,000-$30,000 for the same course.  

6. Enoxaparin (Lovenox) - Blood Thinner
   - U.S. Price: A single syringe can cost up to $800.  
   - Other Countries:  
     - UK: ~$7.30 per syringe.

The Pharmacy Benefit Manager Transparency Act (S.526) cracks down on spread pricing schemes where PBMs charge insurers more than they pay pharmacies, keeping the difference. Section 2(a)(1) bans this practice unless 100% of rebates go to health plans.

Meanwhile, the Protecting Pharmacies in Medicaid Act targets $2.2B in savings by ending PBM clawbacks and mandating transparent reimbursements.

Congress must pass these reforms to stop shadowy pricing games—taxpayers and patients deserve accountability, not more bureaucratic profiteering.
